'Fifty-one,' said Dhruv, tapping the notebook. 'That's how many ways the food-truck idea can collapse.'
'Fifty-one?' said Vidya, flipping pages. 'Fuel, permits, rain, a rival, a bad cook, a stolen generator...'
'Right. And each one is possible. I feel sick reading it.'
'Which is the most likely?'
'I don't know. They all look equally bad.'
'So how do you decide what to worry about first?'
Dhruv closed the notebook. 'I don't. Maybe I shouldn't start.'
'You haven't even tried one weekend.'
'Fifty-one reasons, Vidya.'
Vidya sighed. 'Reasons, sure. But you haven't marked which are likely or which would hurt most. It's just a heap.'

qa.a: Dhruv could mark each risk for how likely it is and how much damage it does, keep the top few, and run one small weekend test.

qa.a: Vidya sees it as a heap without ranking and not a reason to quit, and the sigh suggests some frustration.

passage:
I'm Rekha, and last winter I wanted to start a tiffin delivery service for students in our area.
A mentor told me to do a pre-mortem: imagine it has failed and list why. So I did, on a Sunday night. Cooks quit. Food goes bad. Hostel bans outside food. Scooter breaks down. Payment app fails. Students go home for holidays. Competitor opens. Rent rises. I didn't stop. By two in the morning I had fifty-three reasons across four pages.
I read them in a row and felt sick. Every line seemed equally likely, equally fatal. I never sorted them, never asked which ones mattered.
My friend Nilesh asked a week later, "So when do you start?" I said I was still researching risks.
That was February. It's October now. The four pages are still in my drawer, and I still haven't cooked a single tiffin.

qa.q: How many reasons did Rekha list by two in the morning?
qa.a: Rekha listed fifty-three reasons across four pages.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling after reading the list in a row?
qa.a: Rekha felt sick with dread, because every reason seemed equally likely and fatal.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Rekha better than listing every risk?
qa.a: Rekha could rank the risks by how likely and how harmful each is, deal with the top few, and start with a small trial of ten tiffins.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see Rekha's answer that the risks were still being researched?
qa.a: Nilesh may sense the research has become a way of putting off starting, and feel sorry that the idea is stuck.

grounding: It shows a student listing dozens of ways a venture could fail without ranking them, so the exercise turns into dread and a reason not to begin.

Incubation cell note, 14 March
Sonali came in today for her fortnightly check-in about the book-exchange startup. Last time I asked her to try a pre-mortem.
She brought a file. Sixty-two failure points, typed, numbered. Some were serious: nobody signs up, the college bans sales in the hostel. Others were things like "the printer breaks" and "someone spills tea on the books". She had given them all the same weight.
She said she had not slept properly all week and was thinking of dropping the idea. She has not yet spoken to a single possible user.
I realised I had given her half a tool. I took a red pen, drew two columns for likely and damaging, and we rated the first ten together.
She will rank the rest and bring the top five next time. Salma, her co-founder, will run a ten-person trial meanwhile.
— Faculty mentor

qa.q: How many failure points were in Sonali's file?
qa.a: There were sixty-two failure points, typed and numbered.

qa.q: How was Sonali feeling during the week before the check-in?
qa.a: She was anxious and overwhelmed, not sleeping properly and thinking of dropping the idea.

qa.q: What else could the mentor have told Sonali when first suggesting the pre-mortem?
qa.a: The mentor could have asked her to rate each risk for likelihood and damage from the start, so the list would guide action instead of causing fear.

qa.q: How might Salma be affected by the new plan?
qa.a: Salma gets a clear job, a ten-person trial, which moves the startup forward instead of waiting for every risk to be solved.

grounding: It shows a student listing many unranked failure points for a startup, feeling dread and nearly giving up before starting.
